figures.caption: Making new bonds gives off heat from the reaction to the surroundings

specPoints.text: know that bond-breaking is an endothermic process and that bond-making is an exothermic process
use bond energies to calculate the enthalpy change during a chemical reaction

primer.text: From Energy Level Diagrams you already know how the product level sits below or above the reactant level. This note explains those levels with bonds: breaking costs energy and making pays it back. It finishes by pricing every bond in a reaction to calculate the enthalpy change from scratch.

lessons.title: Breaking costs, making pays
lessons.opening: Every bond is a spring with a price tag: pulling it apart costs energy, snapping it shut pays energy back. This lesson fixes which half of the reaction spends and which one earns.
keyPoints: Bond-breaking is an endothermic process because energy must be taken in to break bonds.
Bond-making is an exothermic process because energy is released when new bonds are formed.
Whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic overall depends on the balance between breaking and making.
Each chemical bond has a specific bond energy for breaking it or forming it.
Bond energies are usually quoted in kilojoules per mole of bonds.

low.restatement: Pulling a bond apart soaks up energy, and letting a bond click together gives energy out. The winner of that tug of war decides whether the whole reaction warms or cools its surroundings.
low.analogy: It is like dismantling and rebuilding scaffolding: taking it down costs effort, and clicking new poles together releases a satisfying snap.
low.examPointer: Quote the pairing in the right order: breaking endothermic, making exothermic.

medium.restatement: Energy must be taken in to break the existing bonds of the reactants, so bond-breaking is endothermic. Energy is released when the new bonds of the products form, so bond-making is exothermic, and the overall sign depends on the difference between the two.
medium.analogy: A demolition crew is paid to pull a wall down, while the builders of the new wall hand energy back as each brick locks in; the site balance is the enthalpy change.
medium.examPointer: Explain the sign of ΔH by comparing energy in to break bonds with energy out making them.

check.stem: Why is bond-breaking classified as endothermic?

options.text: Because energy must be taken in to pull the bond apart
options.explanation: Separating bonded atoms requires supplied energy, which is the endothermic signature.

options.text: Because bonds store heat that escapes
options.explanation: Nothing escapes during breaking; energy is consumed, not released.

options.text: Because broken bonds are unstable
options.explanation: Stability language does not decide the energy direction here.

options.text: Because breaking happens only in cold conditions
options.explanation: Breaking happens whenever energy is supplied, warm or cold.

check.stem: What happens to energy when new bonds form?

options.text: Energy is released, so bond-making is exothermic
options.explanation: Formation of bonds hands energy out to the surroundings.

options.text: Energy is absorbed, so bond-making is endothermic
options.explanation: Absorption belongs to bond-breaking; making pays energy back.

options.text: Energy is unchanged because atoms stay the same
options.explanation: The bonding changes, so the energy changes too.

options.text: Energy becomes light instead of heat
options.explanation: The released energy here is treated as heat given to the surroundings.

check.stem: A reaction overall takes in energy. What does that reveal about its bonds?

options.text: More energy was needed to break bonds than was released making them
options.explanation: An endothermic total means the breaking bill exceeded the making refund.

options.text: More energy was released making bonds than was used breaking them
options.explanation: That balance gives an exothermic total, the opposite of the observation.

options.text: No bonds were broken at all
options.explanation: Some bonds must break for any reaction to happen.

options.text: The bonds were all identical
options.explanation: Bond identity does not force the overall sign.

check.stem: What does the bond energy of a specific bond tell you?

options.text: The energy required to break the bond or given out when it is formed
options.explanation: The two directions carry the same size of energy for that bond.

options.text: The speed at which the bond reacts
options.explanation: Rate is a separate concept from bond energy.

options.text: The temperature needed to start the reaction
options.explanation: That describes activation energy, not the bond energy itself.

options.text: The length of the bond in nanometres
options.explanation: Bond length is a structural property, not an energy.

check.stem: In the phrase ENDothermic, what memory trick does the exam hint attach to bond breaking?

options.text: Bond breaking is endothermic and results in the end of the bond
options.explanation: The hint links the END of the word to the END of the bond.

options.text: Bond breaking happens at the end of a reaction
options.explanation: The trick concerns the word END, not the reaction timeline.

options.text: Endothermic bonds never reform
options.explanation: Bonds can reform; the trick is about breaking.

options.text: Endothermic reactions cannot be reversed
options.explanation: Reversibility is a separate topic.

lessons.title: The overall sign from the bond balance
lessons.opening: Add up the energy spent breaking bonds, add up the energy earned making them, and the difference carries the sign of the reaction. This lesson reads that difference in both directions.
keyPoints: In an exothermic reaction the energy released making bonds is greater than the energy taken in breaking them.
Exothermic reactions have a negative enthalpy change because the reactants hold more energy than the products.
In an endothermic reaction the energy needed to break bonds exceeds the energy released forming them.
Endothermic reactions have a positive enthalpy change because the products hold more energy than the reactants.
The overall enthalpy change equals the energy in minus the energy out.

low.restatement: If making bonds refunds more than breaking spent, the reaction pays heat out and its enthalpy change is negative. If the breaking bill is bigger, heat is soaked up and the change is positive.
low.analogy: A car trip costs fuel to undo parking and earns nothing for re-parking; whether the day cost or earned money is the sign of the journey.
low.examPointer: Compare the two sums explicitly and let the bigger one decide the sign of ΔH.

medium.restatement: When the energy released forming new bonds is greater than the energy taken in breaking old ones, the reaction is exothermic with a negative enthalpy change. When the breaking cost is greater, the reaction is endothermic with a positive enthalpy change.
medium.analogy: Renovating a kitchen: if the resale value of the new fittings beats the demolition bill you profit, just as bond-making beating bond-breaking releases energy.
medium.examPointer: State which sum is larger and then assign the sign; never quote a sign without the comparison behind it.

check.stem: Why does an exothermic reaction carry a negative enthalpy change?

options.text: The reactants hold more energy than the products, so energy left the system
options.explanation: A fall in the energy of the chemicals is written as a negative change.

options.text: Because bond energies are always negative numbers
options.explanation: Bond energies are quoted positive; the sign comes from the balance.

options.text: Because the reaction happened quickly
options.explanation: Rate has no bearing on the sign.

options.text: Because the products are gases
options.explanation: State of the products does not fix the sign.

check.stem: A reaction has a positive enthalpy change. Which bond statement matches it?

options.text: The energy needed to break existing bonds was greater than the energy released forming new ones
options.explanation: A breaking bill larger than the making refund leaves the chemicals richer in energy.

options.text: The energy released forming new bonds was greater than the breaking cost
options.explanation: That describes an exothermic, negative change.

options.text: No bonds were made, only broken
options.explanation: Reactions both break and make bonds.

options.text: All bonds involved had equal energies
options.explanation: Equal energies would give a change near zero, not positive.

check.stem: Two reactions break the same bonds, but reaction 2 forms stronger new bonds. What follows?

options.text: Reaction 2 is more exothermic because forming stronger bonds releases more energy
options.explanation: Bigger making refunds push the balance further negative.

options.text: Reaction 2 is more endothermic
options.explanation: Stronger new bonds make the change more negative, not more positive.

options.text: Both reactions must have the same enthalpy change
options.explanation: The forming side differs, so the totals differ.

options.text: Neither reaction releases energy
options.explanation: At least one could still be exothermic overall.

check.stem: A student says breaking bonds releases energy because sparks fly. What is the correction?

options.text: Breaking bonds takes energy in; any sparks come from energy released elsewhere in the change
options.explanation: The breaking half always absorbs; visible effects belong to the overall process.

options.text: Sparks prove breaking is exothermic
options.explanation: The overall effect and the bond-breaking half are different things.

options.text: Sparks mean the bonds were weak
options.explanation: Bond strength is an energy quantity, not a visibility judgement.

options.text: Sparks only appear in endothermic changes
options.explanation: No such rule exists.

check.stem: Which expression computes the enthalpy change from bond energies?

options.text: Energy taken in to break bonds minus energy given out making bonds
options.explanation: That difference is the overall enthalpy change of the reaction.

options.text: Energy given out making bonds minus energy taken in breaking them
options.explanation: That reverses the sign convention.

options.text: The two energies added together
options.explanation: Adding would double-count rather than compare.

options.text: The two energies multiplied together
options.explanation: Multiplication has no meaning in this balance.

lessons.title: Pricing a reaction with bond energies
lessons.opening: With a table of bond energies, every reaction can be priced like a shopping list: add the breaking costs, add the making refunds, subtract. This lesson runs that arithmetic on one full reaction.
keyPoints: Add together the bond energies of all bonds in the reactants to find the energy in.
Add together the bond energies of all bonds in the products to find the energy out.
The enthalpy change equals the energy in minus the energy out.
Balancing numbers matter, so count how many of each bond are broken or made.
A displayed formula equation helps you spot every bond before counting.

low.restatement: List every bond the reactants own and total their energies, then do the same for the products. Taking the first total away from the second leaves the enthalpy change, with a minus meaning heat was released.
low.analogy: It is like trading in an old bicycle for a new one: add up the parts you give, add up the parts you get, and the difference tells you if you were paid.
low.examPointer: Show the two totals separately before subtracting, and double-check the balancing numbers.

medium.restatement: The energy in is the sum of bond energies for every reactant bond, and the energy out is the same sum for every product bond. Subtracting energy out from energy in gives the enthalpy change, which is negative when more energy is released than consumed.
medium.analogy: Balancing a shop till: everything customers hand over is the energy in, everything handed back in change is the energy out, and the till difference is the enthalpy change.
medium.examPointer: Write the displayed formula equation first, count each bond type with its balancing number, then run the two sums.

check.stem: Why write a displayed formula equation before counting bonds?

options.text: It shows every bond clearly so none are missed when counting
options.explanation: Displayed formulas expose each bond, preventing miscounts before the arithmetic.

options.text: It makes the reaction faster
options.explanation: Writing equations never changes reaction speed.

options.text: It converts the answer to kilojoules
options.explanation: Units come from the bond energy table, not the equation style.

options.text: It proves the reaction is exothermic
options.explanation: The sign comes from the sums, not the drawing.

check.stem: Hydrogen burns: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O. How many H-H bonds are broken?

options.text: Two, one in each hydrogen molecule
options.explanation: The balancing 2 before H2 means two H-H bonds are broken.

options.text: One, because H-H appears once in the formula
options.explanation: The balancing number doubles the count.

options.text: Four, because water has four hydrogens
options.explanation: Water hydrogens belong to O-H bonds being made, not H-H bonds broken.

options.text: Zero, because hydrogen is an element
options.explanation: Element molecules still contain bonds that must break.

check.stem: Energy in is 678 kJ and energy out is 862 kJ. What is the enthalpy change and its meaning?

options.text: -184 kJ, exothermic because more energy was released making bonds than spent breaking them
options.explanation: 678 - 862 gives -184, and the negative value marks an exothermic reaction.

options.text: +184 kJ, endothermic because energy out is bigger
options.explanation: Subtracting in the stated order gives a negative value; the bigger out-sum means release.

options.text: 1540 kJ, because the sums add
options.explanation: The energies are subtracted, never added.

options.text: -862 kJ, ignoring the breaking cost
options.explanation: Both sums enter the subtraction.

check.stem: A bond energy table lists H-Br as 366 kJ. What energy is needed to break all bonds in 2HBr?

options.text: 732 kJ, because two H-Br bonds are broken
options.explanation: The balancing 2 doubles the single-bond energy.

options.text: 366 kJ, because the bond energy applies to the whole equation
options.explanation: Bond energies apply per mole of bonds, so the count matters.

options.text: 183 kJ, because the energy is shared
options.explanation: Energies are not shared between bonds.

options.text: It cannot be found from the table
options.explanation: One multiplication gives it directly.

check.stem: A calculation gives a positive enthalpy change for a reaction run in a burner. What is the most likely slip?

options.text: The subtraction was reversed, taking energy out from energy in the wrong way round
options.explanation: Reversing the subtraction flips the sign; burning should give a negative change.

options.text: The bond energies were read from the wrong row
options.explanation: Possible, but the described flip of sign is the classic subtraction slip.

options.text: The reaction cannot have a positive change
options.explanation: Some reactions do; the burner context makes it unlikely here.

options.text: The table units were joules not kilojoules
options.explanation: Unit errors change size, not sign.

glossary.definition: The energy required to break a specific bond or given out when that bond forms, quoted per mole of bonds.
A change that takes energy in, such as the breaking of chemical bonds.
A change that gives energy out, such as the making of chemical bonds.
The total bond energy of all bonds broken in the reactants during a reaction.
The total bond energy of all bonds formed in the products during a reaction.

workedExample.prompt: Hydrogen reacts with chlorine to form hydrogen chloride gas: H-H + Cl-Cl → 2H-Cl. Bond energies: H-H 436 kJ, Cl-Cl 242 kJ, H-Cl 431 kJ. Calculate the overall energy change and use the value to explain whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.
steps: Energy in to break the reactant bonds: 436 + 242 = 678 kJ
Energy out from forming two H-Cl bonds: 2 x 431 = 862 kJ
The negative value shows energy is being released to the surroundings.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The overall energy change is -184 kJ, so the reaction is exothermic.
